title: The Grammar of the Body: Solesmes to Paris
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: L'Enfant du Cambrésis: The Frozen Cradle (1811–1822)

stops.name: Solesmes, the town of the North
stops.campa: In Solesmes, a little town of the Cambrésis twenty kilometres east of Cambrai, François Alexandre Nicolas Chéri Delsarte is born on the nineteenth of November 1811. The father is an inventor whose contrivances devour the family's money; the mother comes of a better house and watches the fortune drain into failed devices. Into poverty the child is born who will one day chart the whole grammar of the human body. The flat wet fields of the North, the grey light, the hunger already in the house: these are his first teachers of what a body does under want.

stops.name: The road to Paris, the mother's flight
stops.campa: The father's inventions have ruined the house. The mother, of the wealthier line, will not sink with it; she leaves her husband and turns toward Paris to find work, taking the two eldest, François and his brother Louis, and leaving the two youngest with a grandmother. Along the winter roads out of the North the small family goes south toward the capital. It is the great division of the boy's life: the household broken, the road opening, the city ahead that will keep him and kill nearly everyone he brings to it.
suggested_refs: Route de Cambrai à Paris, 19th century

stops.name: Paris, the death of mother and brother
stops.campa: In Paris the plan collapses into grief. The mother sickens and dies; the brother Louis dies after her. The boy is left alone in the enormous city, a child of nine or ten with no house and no protector. The tradition keeps the legend darker still: the brother frozen to death, held against François in the cold. Whether fever or frost took Louis, the fact that shapes everything is the same: the small warm body going cold in his arms, and the survivor turned forever toward the question of what the living body shows and what the dying body ceases to show.

Genevieve Stebbins, Delsarte System of Expression

segments.name: L'Apprenti: The Porcelain and the Hunger (1822–1825)

stops.name: Paris, apprenticed to the porcelain painter
stops.campa: In 1822 François is bound apprentice to a porcelain painter of Paris. He learns the fine steady hand, the placing of a line, the reading of a face onto a plate: a first schooling of the eye in the exact registering of form. But music pulls harder than porcelain. The boy sings; he cannot stop singing; and the apprenticeship to the brush becomes the reluctant antechamber to the apprenticeship to the voice. Already the double gift is in him: the painter's eye that will one day map the body, and the singer's ear that the Conservatoire will ruin.
stops.quote: In 1822, François was apprenticed to a porcelain painter of Paris, but, yielding to a taste and aptitude for music, in the year 1825, he sought and obtained admission to the Conservatory as a pensioner.
stops.quote_source: Biographical note, Delsarte System of Oratory, tr. Frances A. Shaw
suggested_refs: Sèvres decorated porcelain of the Restoration

stops.name: Paris, the starving apprentice and Bambini
stops.campa: The apprentice years are years of hunger; the orphan lives on almost nothing, and the tradition tells of a body pushed to the edge of poisoning by what a starving boy will eat. Into this a deliverer comes: a music professor named Bambini hears the boy sing, recognises the instrument, and opens the way to the Conservatoire. The child who watched his brother die and painted faces onto porcelain to eat is lifted, by an ear that will not let his voice be lost, toward the school that will lose it for him.
suggested_refs: Conservatoire de Paris, rue du Faubourg-Poissonnière

segments.name: La Voix Perdue: The Ruined Voice (1825–1832)

stops.name: Conservatoire de Paris, admission as pensioner
stops.campa: In 1825 Delsarte is admitted to the Paris Conservatoire as a pensioner, placed in the vocal classes. He enters with a true tenor and a hunger to be a great singer. Around him the reigning method is taught by rote and fashion: the forcing of the voice, the borrowed gesture, the artificial style of the age. He obeys the masters. Obeying them, he is destroyed. The very institution meant to make him a singer sets in motion the wound that will unmake the singer and make, in his place, the first law-giver of expression.
stops.quote: He had been placed in the vocal classes, and in consequence of faults in method and direction, he lost his voice.
stops.quote_source: Biographical note, Delsarte System of Oratory, tr. Frances A. Shaw

stops.name: Conservatoire de Paris, the voice breaks
stops.campa: The wound comes due. By the close of the 1820s the forced method has broken the instrument; the tenor is left with a voice ruined by bad teaching, inconsolable, his singer's career wrecked before it began. He will curse the arbitrary, unreasoning schooling of the Conservatoire to the end of his life. Yet from the ashes rises the vow that founds a science: if the masters cannot say WHY the voice is placed thus and the gesture made so, he will find the law himself. The wound turns the singer into a scientist of expression.
stops.quote: He was inconsolable, but, without making light of his sorrow, we may count that loss happy, which gave the world its first law-giver in the art of oratory.
stops.quote_source: Biographical note, Delsarte System of Oratory, tr. Frances A. Shaw

stops.name: Opéra-Comique, the singer with the ruined instrument
stops.campa: For a season Delsarte sings tenor at the Opéra-Comique, choosing his parts to spare the maimed voice, leaning already on the ACTING more than the tone, on the truth of the gesture more than the height of the note. He learns on the boards what the classes never taught: that an audience is moved less by the sound than by its manner, that a true attitude of the body persuades where a forced high note only astonishes. The failed singer is already, on stage, becoming the master of expression.
stops.quote: It is not what we say that persuades, but the manner of saying it.
stops.quote_source: François Delsarte, in Delsarte System of Oratory

segments.name: Le Savant de l'Expression: The Watcher in the City (1830–1839)

stops.name: Jardin des Tuileries, the nurse and the child's thumb
stops.campa: In the Tuileries garden Delsarte watches the nurses and their charges for hours, week upon week, reading the language the body speaks before it knows it speaks. He marks a law in the smallest sign: as love wakes in an infant the fingers loosen and open, and when the true mother clasps the child the thumb springs wide from the hand, while the hired nurse never draws it so. From such minute and patient reading the whole doctrine grows: that every inner state has its outward sign, that gesture never lies, that the body has a grammar as fixed as speech.
stops.quote: Gesture is the direct agent of the heart, the interpreter of speech. It is elliptical discourse.
stops.quote_source: François Delsarte, address before the Philotechnic Society (Sorbonne), in Delsarte System of Oratory
suggested_refs: Delsarte's chart of the hand and thumb

stops.name: Paris, marriage to Rosine Andrien
stops.campa: On the fourth of June 1833 Delsarte marries Rosine Charlotte Andrien, a virtuoso pianist and teacher of solfège at the Conservatoire, of the house of Philippy de Bucelly d'Estrées. She becomes the keeper of the work he will never publish, the accompanist of his salons, the mother of his seven children. Through this marriage and his own sister's line he is bound to music's future: his sister Aimée is mother of Georges Bizet, so the maker of Carmen is the master of expression's own nephew. In 1833 too he prints his first treatise on singing.

stops.name: Hôpitaux de Paris, the wards of the dying
stops.campa: Delsarte goes into the hospital wards to watch the sick and the dying. He learns anatomy, takes courses in medicine, stands by beds to see how the failing body sheds its gestures: which sign goes first, which holds to the last breath. Here he grounds the science: not fancy but observation, the law read off the living and the perishing frame. He will say to depend on inspiration alone is as foolish as waiting for a shipwreck to learn to swim; the swimmer, and the actor, must know the law before the crisis.
stops.quote: To depend entirely upon inspiration is as bad as waiting for a shipwreck to learn how to swim.
stops.quote_source: François Delsarte, attributed, in Rick On Theater / Delsartean tradition

stops.name: The asylums and the graveside, the mad and the grieving
stops.campa: Into the asylums Delsarte goes to read the gestures of the mad, where the mask is torn off and the body speaks without governor; and to the cemeteries, to watch the grieving at open graves, where sorrow moves the frame past all pretence. In parks, cafés, churches, mortuaries, the scenes of disaster, he stations himself wherever feeling seizes the body and writes its sign plainly. From the whole reeling census of Paris he distils the constant: the same emotion draws the same gesture in every frame, and the correspondence can be charted.

segments.name: Le Cours d'Esthétique Appliquée: The Master and the Salons (1839–1867)

stops.name: Paris, the Course of Applied Aesthetics opens
stops.campa: In May 1839 Delsarte opens his Cours d'esthétique appliquée, the Course of Applied Aesthetics: the first systematic training of the expressive body in the Western theatre. To preachers, painters, singers, composers, orators and actors he teaches not tricks but LAW: the science of applied aesthetics, the grammar by which every inner state finds its true outward form. What the Conservatoire could not tell him, the WHY of gesture and tone, he now tells the age. The failed tenor has become the law-giver, and Paris comes to be taught its own body.
stops.quote: Eloquence is a means, not an end. We must not love art for its own sake, that would be idolatry. Art gives wings for ascent to God.
stops.quote_source: François Delsarte, in Delsarte System of Oratory

stops.name: The studio, the Law of Correspondence and the Trinity
stops.campa: In the studio the doctrine takes its shape. Man is threefold, life, mind, soul, after the image of the Trinity; and so his every faculty divides in three: the vocal, the buccal, and the gesture, the languages of what he feels, thinks and loves. The primary law is Correspondence: to each spiritual function answers a bodily form, eccentric, concentric or normal, so that from three genera spring nine species: the Universal Criterion that governs voice, speech and gesture alike. He teaches that gesture, being parallel with the impression, must always come first; speech is only reflected expression, after the fact.
stops.quote: Man says what he feels by inflections of the voice, what he loves by gesture, what he thinks by articulate speech.
stops.quote_source: François Delsarte, address before the Philotechnic Society, tr. Stebbins
suggested_refs: Delsarte's chart of the Universal Criterion
The Delsarte cross / ninefold accords diagram

stops.name: The studio, the nine attitudes and the zones
stops.campa: The grammar is drawn as a map on the living frame. The body divides into three zones: the head, mental; the torso, moral and emotive; the limbs, vital and physical. Every region bears its own ninefold accord, three directions crossed with three, so that the head alone owns nine attitudes, each the exact sign of a state of soul. Statics, dynamics, semiotics: the body at rest, the body in motion, the body as sign. What porcelain and hospital and Tuileries taught the eye is now set down as the Delsarte cross, the geometry of the expressive man.
stops.quote: Gesture must always precede speech. In fact, speech is reflected expression. It must come after gesture, which is parallel with the impression received.
stops.quote_source: François Delsarte, in Delsarte System of Oratory
suggested_refs: Nine attitudes of the head, engraved plates
Delsarte's zone chart of the body

stops.name: The salons, the great pupils gather
stops.campa: The famous course draws the age to Delsarte's rooms. The tragedienne Rachel comes; the English tragedian Macready; the singer Jenny Lind; the preacher Père Hyacinthe; the composers Gounod and Bizet cross his circle. He coaches orator and actor and priest to wed the inner feeling to the true gesture, to stop the forced style the Conservatoire had bred in him. In the salons he demonstrates rather than writes, singing the old airs with his ruined voice and moving so truly that hearers weep: the doctrine transmitted mouth to ear, body to eye, never fixed in a book.

stops.name: The court, recitals before the kings
stops.campa: The failed tenor sings before thrones. Delsarte performs at the courts of Louis-Philippe and of Napoleon III, drawing from a wrecked voice, by pure truth of expression, what golden throats cannot; France gives him the Legion of Honour. He proves in his own maimed person the whole thesis of his science: that the manner, the attitude, the felt and lawful gesture, moves the heart where mere sound fails. The wound of the Conservatoire is vindicated at the Tuileries palace: the ruined singer, become the master of expression, is honoured for the very lack that made him.
suggested_refs: Court of Napoleon III, Tuileries Palace

stops.name: The Sorbonne, the address before the Philotechnic Society
stops.campa: At the Sorbonne, before the Philotechnic Society of Paris, Delsarte delivers the one lecture the tradition keeps whole: the manuscript his widow will one day yield to his American heirs. There, in his own words, he sets the definitions the disciples will carry: gesture the direct agent of the heart, elliptical discourse; the three languages of feeling, thought and love; art not for itself but as wings for the ascent to God. The man who would not publish speaks his doctrine aloud once, plainly, and the spoken words become the scripture of the movement he founds.
stops.quote: Gesture is more than speech. It is the fit manifestation of feeling. It is the revealer of thought and the commentator upon speech.
stops.quote_source: François Delsarte, address before the Philotechnic Society of Paris

segments.name: L'Héritier d'Amérique: The Doctrine Crosses the Sea (1869–1871)

stops.name: Paris, Steele MacKaye at the master's feet
stops.campa: In October 1869 the young American Steele MacKaye comes to Paris and gives himself to Delsarte, studying with the master every day through to July 1870. The old man, ill and out of fashion, pours the unpublished science into this one devoted heir: the zones, the accords, the criterion, the whole grammar he never set in a book. To MacKaye he entrusts his papers and his trust. The disciple who will carry the doctrine across the ocean is being made in the very rooms where the war is about to fall.
suggested_refs: MacKaye's notebooks of the Delsarte lessons

stops.name: New York and Boston, the system reaches America
stops.campa: The war has driven MacKaye home. In March 1871, while the master lies dying in besieged Paris, the disciple mounts the platform in New York and Boston and introduces to America the Delsarte System: the first stone of every school of dance and drama that will rise from it. What Delsarte would not publish crosses the sea as living practice, adding harmonic gymnastics of MacKaye's own devising. The doctrine that began in a Tuileries garden, watching a child's thumb, now takes root in the New World even as its author's life runs out in the Old.

segments.name: La Mort dans Paris Assiégée: The Siege and the Grave (1870–1871)

stops.name: Paris, the siege closes round the master
stops.campa: On the nineteenth of September 1870 the Prussian armies close the ring around Paris. Through the long hungry winter of the siege and into the burning spring of the Commune, the old master, ill and broken and out of fashion, holds on in the starving city. The empire whose court once honoured him has fallen; the pupils are scattered; the disciple is fled overseas. The scientist of the dying body now watches his own city die around him: the shells, the famine, the fire. He reads, in the great collective grief of Paris, the last confirmation of his lifelong law.

stops.name: Paris, the death of François Delsarte
stops.campa: On the twentieth of July 1871, in the wrecked and smoking aftermath of the Commune, François Delsarte dies in Paris: ill, broken, out of fashion, the great system still unpublished in his own hand. The failed tenor who lost his voice and gained a science, who read the law of the body off the dying and the grieving and a child's spread thumb, goes to his own death having given the whole movement-lineage its root. He is buried in the cemetery of Montmartre. The doctrine survives only because his widow keeps the papers and his heirs, across the sea, keep the practice.
stops.quote: Art gives wings for ascent to God.
stops.quote_source: François Delsarte, in Delsarte System of Oratory
suggested_refs: Genevieve Stebbins, Delsarte System of Expression (1885)

stops.name: The world after: Stebbins, Laban, Muybridge and the notated body
stops.campa: The root sends up the tree. Genevieve Stebbins, MacKaye's pupil, obtains the Sorbonne manuscript from the widow and in 1885 publishes the Delsarte System of Expression, spreading harmonic gymnastics through America; from that soil rise Isadora Duncan, Ruth St. Denis, and the whole of modern dance. Laban will notate the moving body; Muybridge will freeze its every gesture in the frame; the grammar of expression Delsarte derived becomes the common inheritance of dance, film and theatre. The man who never published is the acknowledged father of the notated, expressive body.
suggested_refs: Genevieve Stebbins, Delsarte System of Expression (1885)
